newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Two Congos exchange shell fire, radio says.
newsitem.headline: Two Congos exchange shell fire, radio says.

text.p: Troops fired mortar bombs from Kinshasa into neighbouring Congo Republic in retaliation for firing from there, state radio in Kinshasa said on Thursday.
"Shells from Brazzaville fell on Tuesday on the seminary...leaving two wounded, including a little girl seriously," La Voix du Peuple radio said.
"The Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire) retaliated towards the Bacongo and Makelekele districts of Brazzaville," it added.
The radio said the seminary was near the palace of former dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, ousted by Laurent Kabila in May.

Brazzaville, the capital of Congo Republic, has been the scene of fighting since June between political factions allied to President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguessou. It lies across the river from Kinshasa.
Kinshasa radio did not say which side fired the shells from Brazzaville, but a Brazzaville-based radio station controlled by Lissouba on Wednesday laid the blame on Sassou.

"Kinshasa sent over to Brazzaville about 10 shells that fell on the Bacongo, Makelekele and Mfilou districts, causing a wave of panic," the radio quoted presidential spokesman Edmond Philippe Galli as saying.
The radio said Kabila's troops acted in retaliation to five shells fired at Kinshasa by forces loyal to Sassou.
Kabila's government threatened "military measures" against Brazzaville when shells landed in Kinshasa in the past.
An uneasy truce in Brazzaville has been disturbed by exchanges of fire in recent days, and further shelling inside the capital was heard on Thursday.
Residents said shells landed on the Bacongo district of Brazzaville on Wednesday afternoon, fired from the area around the Presidency.
Bacongo is the only district of Brazzaville to have remained largely unaffected by the conflict. It is full of refugees from other parts of town.
Kabila said after a regional summit in Kinshasa on Wednesday that he and the presidents of Uganda and Rwanda wanted to cooperate on a peace proposal for Congo-Brazzaville.
Despite the renewed firing in Brazzaville, diplomats say they still expect Congo peace talks to resume in the Gabonese capital of Libreville in coming days.
The talks have stalled over the choice of a prime minister to head an interim government and what powers he should have.
